claims.text: Formation and crystal-structure selection in noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements are governed primarily by atomic size mismatch and mixing entropy.
Increasing atomic size mismatch beyond a critical threshold destabilizes the single-phase solid solution.
Destabilization caused by excessive atomic size mismatch leads to phase separation or elemental segregation.
High mixing entropy favors the single-phase solid-solution state.
Slower heating and cooling permit greater atomic diffusion and equilibration.
Greater diffusion and equilibration during slower thermal processing promote single-phase formation.
Rapid thermal cycling increases the likelihood of phase separation.
Rapid thermal cycling increases the likelihood of uncontrolled particle morphology.
Large atomic size mismatch increases lattice strain.
Lattice strain caused by large atomic size mismatch reduces the stability of the single-phase solid solution.
Mixing entropy counteracts the destabilizing effect of size-mismatch-induced lattice strain.
Slow thermal processing reduces kinetic impediments to forming a single-phase solid solution.
Reducing atomic size mismatch and using slower thermal regimes will promote single-phase solid-solution formation relative to the baseline.
Increasing atomic size mismatch and using rapid thermal cycling will increase phase separation, elemental segregation, and uncontrolled morphology relative to the baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies to equiatomic or near-equiatomic noble metal–based nanoparticles containing more than five elements and synthesized under inert atmosphere.
The proposed mechanism does not apply to non-noble-metal HEAs, systems with fewer than five elements, or highly non-equiatomic compositions.

contradictions.description: The intervention requires atomic size mismatch to be varied at fixed overall composition, but the proposed means is element substitution. Substituting constituent elements changes the chemical composition, even if elemental ratios remain equiatomic, so the stated fixed-composition control is not maintained.
